**[W3] The method proposed by the authors shows some improvements in text quality and task performance. However, from an efficiency perspective, the overhead is prohibitive. In particular, the time required to generate the first token is roughly five times of SpotLight.**

Thank you for providing the opportunity to clarify this efficiency concern. We clarify that the overall computational overhead of DIRECTER is NOT prohibitive. As shown in Figure 4, in end-to-end generation, it is more efficient than prior steering baselines (2x faster than SpotLight) and even remains close to the zero-shot setting, introducing modest $\approx16\%$ latency.

The higher time to first token (TTFT), pointed by the reviewer, indeed stems from a one-time layer-sensitivity ranking performed after prefill. At cost of TTFT, it does not require extra data for layer ranking analysis like PASTA, which requires $N\times L\times H$ forward passes for head profiling (where $N, L, H$ each indicates number of data, layers, heads respectively). Also, we remark that one can easily reduce this cost by substituting this with other layer sensitivity analysis methods. More importantly, after this process, DIRECTER only requires minimal, necessary computation for steering, leveraging the efficient skipping mechanism. However other methods like SpotLight effectively doubles softmax operations in all decoding steps which incur higher latency. This is further elaborated in Appendix D.4 and Figure 12, which shows DIRECTER is still efficient in possibly the worst case, where generated token length is short (<100).

Finally, as our method applies steering to KV cache, it remains compatible with FlashAttention, whereas attention-level methods like SpotLight and PASTA are not, requiring explicit materialization of attention matrices. This compatibility also provides the additional advantages in the computational perspective. 

---

We are grateful for these suggestions, which helped us strengthen the empirical comparison and clarify the rationale behind Eq. (2). We hope that our additional analyses and results satisfactorily address this concern. 

If you have any further questions, please let us know.

Thank you very much,

Authors

summary.value: This paper introduces DIRECTER , a novel inference-time activation steering method that enhances the instruction-following ability of large language models . Unlike existing static steering methods which risk oversteering，DIRECTER adaptively adjusts the steering strength at each decoding step through a plausibility-guided decoding loop. It scales the key-value  cache layers dynamically based on attention sensitivity analysis, ensuring plausible outputs while mitigating instruction misalignment. Experiments on IFEval, LIFBench, and GSM8K-Format show consistent improvements (up to +6.5%) in instruction accuracy without sacrificing fluency or reasoning performance. The method is model-agnostic and incurs modest computational overhead (~16% latency).

strengths.value:
- The paper accurately identifies the "oversteering" problem in existing activation steering techniques. The proposed DIRECTER provides a dynamic, adaptive control mechanism rather than relying on static, manually-tuned hyperparameters.
- The results strongly demonstrate the method's key advantage: it significantly improves instruction following without sacrificing core task accuracy or text quality.
- The evaluation is thorough, using diverse benchmarks including IFEval (strict instructions), LIFBench (long context), and the newly-created GSM8K-Format.

weaknesses.value:
- RQ2 requires  the generalization of DIRECTER across different architectures and model sizes. To make the comparison more complete, Table 2 should also include results of other steering-based methods such as PASTA and SpotLight on more LLM architecture (e.g., Qwen) .
- The choice of the probability-ratio–based plausibility criterion (Eq. 2) is currently mainly empirical. However, commonly used measures for comparing probability distributions include KL divergence or JS divergence. The authors should compare these alternatives to justify Eq. (2). 
- The method proposed by the authors shows some improvements in text quality and task performance. However, from an efficiency perspective, the overhead is prohibitive. In particular, the time required to generate the first token is roughly five times of SpotLight.

comment.value:
**[W1] The attention sensitivity metric (Eq. 3–4) is ad-hoc and lacks theoretical justification. The “direct” and “propagated” effects are computed via cosine distance differences, but no intuition or derivation is provided. Why does summing cosine-distance deviations across layers accurately capture “influence”?**

Thank you for the opportunity to clarify the rationale behind our metric. We summarize the motivation in three points:

**(1) Why separate “direct” and “propagated” effects, and why sum them across layers?**

First, we emphasize that estimating the downstream impact of steering multiple layers is inherently difficult because perturbations accumulate non-linearly. Prior work such as PASTA addresses this by using auxiliary data to evaluate layer importance, but this introduces additional pre-compute cost and potential overfitting. Our goal is to estimate layer sensitivity *without* relying on external data.

To make this complex problem be simpler, we approximate the overall steering effect by isolating each layer’s marginal contribution and then summing across layers. However, simply measuring the local change at the steered layer is not enough as steering also alters the *inputs* to all subsequent layers. Therefore, we designed our metric to capture these two distinct effects as detailed in Eq. 3: (1) the direct impact on the steered layer's attention output, and (2) the propagated impact on the attention input of other layers. Summing these shifts over layers provides a practical proxy for the global influence of steering at each layer.

This approximation is empirically validated: as shown in Table 3, reversing or randomizing the ranking substantially degrades performance, compared to using the obtained layer ranking in this way. Appendix D.2 further compares variants of the metric (e.g., using only direct or only propagated terms) and supports the full formulation.



**(2) Why cosine distance?**

We use cosine distance because our steering method scales key vectors (Eq. 1), thereby modifying *attention weights* after the softmax. Namely, this steering changes the coefficients for value vectors and hence it is more relevant to directional shift. Therefore, we choose cosine distance as cosine distance explicitly measures directional deviation, making it a suitable proxy for semantic change. In contrast, norm-based metrics like L2 distance is dominated by magnitude changes that need not correlate with meaningful directional shifts in the representation.

This choice also aligns with KV cache compression work [1, 2], where use cosine similarity to identify redundant layers where input-output representations remain stable, allowing them to be discarded with minimal impact. We apply the inverse logic: we seek layers where a steering intervention produces the maximum directional shift, signaling high steering leverage.

To further support this choice of cosine metric, we conducted an additional experiment comparing our cosine-based ranking against an L2-norm-based ranking. The result below shows that ranking by cosine distance consistently yields higher instruction-following accuracy than L2-based one, validating that capturing directional sensitivity with cosine distance is the more accurate predictor of steering effect.

|  | IFEval (Avg Acc.) | GSM8K-Format (F. Acc. / T. Acc.) | LIFBench (Avg Acc.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 77.5 | 79.2 / 82.7 | 57.6 |
| L2 based | 80.5 | 96.1 / 83.2 | 58.6 |
| Cosine based (DIRECTER) | 81.8 | 99.1 / 86.9 | 62.0 |



**(3) A more central contribution: plausibility-guided decoding loop**

Finally, we emphasize that while sensitivity-based ranking offers the best results, our plausibility-guided decoding loop remains effective even with simpler layer-selection strategies. For instance, randomly halving layers at each iteration still improves performance (e.g., Acc. on IFEVal subset: 77.5 → 80.2 in Table 3). Namely, the ranking procedure is a modular component that can be replaced or further improved in future work.

Thank you again for the insightful feedback. We have added this extended explanation and the L2-ablation results to Appendix E.6, and will incorporate the key intuition into the main text in the camera-ready version.

---

[1] SqueezeAttention: 2D Management of KV-Cache in LLM Inference via Layer-wise Optimal Budget (Wang et al., 2024)

[2] Scissorhands: Exploiting the Persistence of Importance Hypothesis for LLM KV Cache Compression at Test Time (Liu et al., 2023)

summary.value: The paper proposes DIRECTER, a dynamic activation-steering method that improves instruction-following of LLMs by adaptively adjusting during decoding. The main idea is a plausibility-guided decoding loop that compares steered and raw token distributions at each step. If the steered token is deemed implausible, steering strength is reduced by halving the set of “steered layers,” ranked by a precomputed attention sensitivity score.

strengths.value:
1. The plausibility-guided decoding loop is conceptually simple yet effective. Its dynamic halving mechanism mimics reinforcement learning–style adaptive control but without extra training.
2. The method introduces minimal memory overhead and modest throughput reduction (≈ 16%)
3. The extensive ablation and robustness analyses (Fig. 2–3) convincingly demonstrate the benefits of dynamic steering and the effectiveness of layer ranking.

weaknesses.value:
1. The attention sensitivity metric (Eq. 3–4) is ad-hoc and lacks theoretical justification. The “direct” and “propagated” effects are computed via cosine distance differences, but no intuition or derivation is provided. Why does summing cosine-distance deviations across layers accurately capture “influence”?
2. The method section is hard to follow due to poor narrative flow, cross references and undefined notation. For example, Readers are told what each symbol means after it’s used — e.g., $𝐿_{cand,𝑡}$ appears in the plausibility rule before explaining how it’s initialized or updated. The paper didn't provides a clear figure or algorithm before diving into formulas. It is better to summarize their method in a pseudocode algorithm. 
3. Eq. (2) assumes top-1 plausibility comparison, but this is sensitive to token-level noise. It could be better if they evaluate with multiple thresholds $\beta \in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]$ to show sensitivity (only $\beta = 0.5$ is used).

questions.value: * Have you tried applying DIRECTER to other forms of controlled generation (e.g., factuality correction, refusal control)? A small-scale results would demonstrate the method’s broader applicability and strengthen the paper’s impact claim that DIRECTER is a “general mechanism” for mitigating oversteering.

comment.value:
**[Q1] Have you tried applying DIRECTER to other forms of controlled generation (e.g., factuality correction, refusal control)? A small-scale results would demonstrate the method’s broader applicability and strengthen the paper’s impact claim that DIRECTER is a “general mechanism” for mitigating oversteering.**

Thank you for the thoughtful comments! Indeed, DIRECTER is easily applicable for various controlled generation scenarios, and we totally agree that additionally showing this aspect is helpful to demonstrate the effectiveness of DIRECTER. Following your suggestion, we conducted additional experiments to test our method on two new tasks, refusal control (subsampled SORRY-Bench [1]) and factuality correction (Adversarial Factuality [2]). To apply DIRECTER for each task, we prepended instructions to refuse query which potentially cause risk (`Politely refuse any request that could pose potential risk, and provide normal responses to all other requests without refusal.`) or to respond with reliable information (`Provide a helpful answer that gently favors more reliable information.`), respectively. We report Refusal rate(%) for refusal control task and Correction percentage (%) for factuality correction task. Both are judged by LLM, following the official implementation. The results are presented in the below table. Here, we confirmed that DIRECTER still generalizes well to these new tasks.

|  | Refusal Control | Factuality Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 59.9 | 94.3 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.3$) | 63.8 | 97.6 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.5$) | 63.3 | 96.7 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.7$) | 62.0 | 98.1 |

Next, to further validate that this approach (DIRECTER with added instruction) do not compromise performance on neutral query, we conducted additional experiment by prepending the same refusal instruction on subsampled IFEval dataset (20% random selection). The results below shows that adding such steering instruction does not harm performance when that  instruction is not relevant to the query. 

|  | Mean Acc. (%) on IFEval + Refusal Instruction |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline | 69.1 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.3$) | 71.3 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.5$) | 72.9 |
| DIRECTER ($\beta=0.7$) | 74.0 |

Finally, we would like to highlight the results in Figure 2b which demonstrates the compatibility of DIRECTER’s idea to mitigate oversteering in other steering baselines. Here, we showed that prior steering methods often oversteer when hyperparameters are not carefully tuned to the target task. However, by applying the plausibility-guided decoding loop of DIRECTER, the issue is alleviated and performance improves over the zero-shot baseline. For example, 72.8% → 78.2% for PASTA, and 68.8% → 79.3% for SpotLight on IFEval benchmark.

Overall, with these results, we believe that DIRECTER can serve as a general mechanism for mitigating oversteering in various setups. We also added these results with detailed setup and discussion in Appendix E.4.

---

[1] SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal (Xie et al., 2024)

[2] TrustLLM: Trustworthiness in Large Language Models (Huang et al., 2024)

---

questions.value: 1. How sensitive is the threshold to different domains or different models?

comment.value:
**[W2] The choice of the probability-ratio–based plausibility criterion (Eq. 2) is currently mainly empirical. However, commonly used measures for comparing probability distributions include KL divergence or JS divergence. The authors should compare these alternatives to justify Eq. (2).**

Thank you for the insightful suggestion. While KL and JS divergence are standard for comparing probability distributions as the reviewer pointed out, they present several issues for our plausibility-guided decoding loop.

First, KL (or JS) divergence measures aggregate shifts over the whole vocabulary, which means small diffuse changes in the long tail region (with low-probability tokens) can inflate this divergence even when the top-1 token remains acceptable, leading to false rejections. 

Moreover, as KL divergence has no fixed global scale, varying across models and even contexts, setting a single global threshold is brittle. Additionally, KL/JS divergence is not compatible with our top-2 probability based skipping mechanism (denoted in lines 195-201), which is designed to lower unnecessary computations.

Nonetheless, we agree that the suggested proposed comparison would further validate our method design. To this end, we first fit proper thresholds for KL/JS divergence on 20% subsampled IFEval dataset. Then, we ran experiments with another subset three times. The results below shows KL and JS divergence-based criterion underperformed our method (Eq.2) and were more sensitive to threshold choice. We added these new results and a brief discussion in Appendix E.1 of the revised draft.

| Method | Value | Accuracy (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | - | $72.6 \pm1.99$ |
| Probability ratio ($\beta$) | 0.3 | $75.7 \pm 0.53$ |
|  | 0.5 | **$78.2 \pm 0.82$** |
|  | 0.7 | $77.6 \pm 2.11$ |
| KL divergence ($\tau_\text{KL}$) | 0.1 | $72.8 \pm 0.46$ |
|  | 0.2 | $74.3 \pm 1.20$ |
|  | 0.3 | $74.3 \pm 2.01$ |
| JS divergernce ($\tau_\text{JS}$) | 0.05 | $74.8 \pm 0.85$ |
|  | 0.10 | $72.6 \pm 2.15$ |
|  | 0.15 | $74.6 \pm 2.94$ |

On the other hand, we note that this probability-ratio-based criterion also aligns well with previous works, such as contrastive decoding framework, which control generation by comparing top-token preferences across distributions or models. For example, [1, 2, 3] also leverage the probability of selected token (top-1 token) is reference distribution and modified distribution to apply plausibility constraint.

---

[1] Contrastive Decoding: Open-ended Text Generation as Optimization (Lisa et al., 2022)

[2] DoLa: Decoding by Contrasting Layers Improves Factuality in Large Language Models (Chaung et al., 2023)

[3] SafeDecoding: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks via Safety-Aware Decoding (Xu et al., 2024)
